newsitem.title: HONG KONG: DMG says property oversupply weighing on Asia.
newsitem.headline: DMG says property oversupply weighing on Asia.

text.p: Contemplating an exports turnaround offers only short relief for Asian bulls keen to see the region return quickly to the dynamic economic performance of the past, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell says.
Property oversupply in some Asian nations risks unleashing disinflationary forces that could well undermine nominal income growth just as the first signs of an exports improvement emerge.
"We conclude that there indeed has been overbuilding, leading to supply outstripping demand -- significantly in some cases," DMG said in a research report dated May 5.
"The risk is that significant disinflationary forces will be released on ASEAN economies resulting in much lower nominal income growth (even as the export cycle turns up as expected)."
ASEAN groups Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, Brunei and Singapore.
Recent tightening by central banks across Southeast Asia was fully justified but probably came too late, the report said.

Asian real estate developers have been unrealistic in their projections, with office space supply rising dramatically between the periods 1990-1994 and 1995-1999. A classic example is the Philippines, which notched up a 201 percent increase.

"This sort of supply is highly unlikely to be matched by a proportionate increase in demand based on projections of real GDP (gross domestic product) growth, suggesting that a situation of oversupply is inevitable in the next two years," DMG said.

Ultimately, loan growth lies at the heart of this issue, the report said. The risk of default on debt borrowed to fund this massive construction boom threatens to unleash disinflationary forces upon Asian economies, it said.
"The combination of persistent capital inflows, poor banking sector corporate governance and financial deregulation has led to bank loan growth of 40 percent across ASEAN," DMG said.

The situation has been worsened in many economies by open capital accounts and pegged currencies, which prevent the central bank from raising interest rates to counter the inflationary effect of inflows.
Country comparisons with Thailand are inevitable, especially as the region confronts rising interest rates in the United States.
But DMG said that while the share of property loans to GDP has risen across the region, other Southeast Asian countries are not in such a serious position.
"The distortions in bank lending from the wrong cost of capital and foreign borrowing exposure are far less elsewhere," the report said.
"But, even without the foreign exposure, the disinflationary impact of excess property supply is likely to be depressing for the markets until the monetary authorities opt for easier policy."
After Thailand's experience, Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines all took preventative action, such as restricting the allowable percentage of property loans to total loans.
In all cases, stock markets fell sharply, with Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines reporting declines of 9.1 percent, 11.3 percent and 17.8 percent from January 1 to May 3, it said.

"Investors are clearly concerned about the short-term constraint on liquidity and profitability, although the central bank measures are without doubt necessary to restore the long-term health of the property market and the overall econmy," DMG said.
"Markets are likely to recover only when central banks move to offset this liquidity squeeze, beginning with lower exchange rates and allowing more flexibility in the setting of monetary policy."
-- Sarah Davison (852) 2843 6470
